analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal ban on evicting tenants during the pandemic and bars it from returning without new law.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 25 Republican cosponsors but never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have canceled the federal ban on most residential evictions that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention put in place during the COVID-19 pandemic, ending it on July 1, 2021. It would also have barred the agency from issuing the same ban again unless Congress passed a new law authorizing it. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had passed, landlords — particularly owners of rental housing who said they could not remove tenants who stopped paying rent — would have been able to resume evictions starting July 1, 2021, and would have recovered the power to reclaim their units, with any future federal eviction ban requiring a new act of Congress. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have restored landlords' ability to evict tenants who stopped paying rent, ending the federal order that barred most residential evictions during the COVID-19 emergency as of July 1, 2021.

It would have prevented the CDC from reissuing the same eviction ban in the future unless Congress passed a new law specifically authorizing it, addressing landlords' concern that the order could be repeatedly extended.

analysis.who_pays: Renters behind on rent during the pandemic would bear the cost: they would lose the federal protection that kept landlords from removing them, and could face eviction for unpaid rent. Public health officials would also lose a tool they used to slow COVID-19 spread, which was the stated reason for the original order. [S3]

drawbacks.text: Nullifying the order on July 1, 2021 would have stripped eviction protection from renters who had lost income during the pandemic, exposing households behind on rent to removal while the emergency was ongoing.

The CDC had issued the order to prevent the spread of COVID-19, and the bill would have blocked that public-health tool without any replacement measure, which is the core objection a supporter would have to answer.

Small landlords genuinely bore losses while tenants could not be removed for unpaid rent, and the bill offered them no relief such as rent assistance, addressing only the eviction side of the problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits went to property owners who wanted to remove nonpaying tenants, while its costs — homelessness risk, disrupted households, and loss of a pandemic public-health measure — fell on renters and the public. Congress already had rental-assistance programs as an alternative path to relieve landlords without evicting tenants during an emergency, and this bill did not connect ending the moratorium to any such support. As written, it traded a broad public protection for a benefit concentrated among landlords.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress without a hearing or vote, and expired when the session ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Duncan introduced the bill on June 28, 2021, joined by 25 Republican cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to the Health Subcommittee the next day; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
The bill would have nullified the CDC eviction order beginning July 1, 2021, and barred any substantially similar order unless a new law specifically authorized it.
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Renters who relied on the federal eviction ban were better off because the bill died, since the protection it targeted stayed in place through this Congress. Landlords pushing to nullify the order gained nothing from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Jeff Duncan
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to nullify the CDC eviction moratorium and referred it to committee

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone and the House Energy and Commerce Committee majority
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referring it to the Health Subcommittee, leaving it to die without a hearing or vote

sides.party_line_note: All 26 initial backers, including the sponsor and all 25 cosponsors, were Republicans, and the bill received no floor vote before Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill's central purpose was to let landlords evict tenants who were protected from removal during the pandemic, shifting the burden of unpaid rent onto renters and public health. Its benefit to property owners came directly at the cost of the people the moratorium shielded.

industries.industry: Property management and real estate operations
industries.note: Property management firms operating rental housing stood to gain the ability to remove nonpaying tenants once the federal halt ended. Their gain came at the expense of tenants' housing security.
